items.title: DoubleTake: Focused Verification of Visual Evidence for Long-Document Understanding
items.text: In long-document question answering, a vision-language model can answer incorrectly even when the retrieved pages contain sufficient evidence. Rereading those pages with the original question gives the model little guidance about which fact to check. We introduce DoubleTake, a training-free framework for focused verification of visual evidence. An initial reading produces a candidate answer and a separate evidence record that guides retrieval for a second reading. A planner compares the two candidates and their supporting evidence to formulate a factual question. A verifier answers it from the source images without seeing either candidate or evidence record, and a reasoner uses this observation to resolve the original question. With a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone, DoubleTake achieves the highest overall accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of four benchmarks. With the same pages and number of model calls, asking a focused factual question yields higher accuracy on all four benchmarks than asking the original question again. Our code is available at https://github.com/small-code-cat/double_take.

items.title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language
items.text: The automated transformation of unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams remains a challenging task, due to linguistic ambiguity and the difficulty to detect non-adjacent control-flow relationships. items.text: Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce HALO, a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. items.title: GH-AWTrace: A Large-Scale Dataset of GitHub Agentic Workflow Execution Logs
items.text: Agentic workflows enable AI agents to perform recurring repository tasks on schedules or in response to repository events. Existing studies examine workflow definitions and outputs, but provide limited evidence of what happens during execution. We present GH-AWTrace, a dataset linking 25,014 verified GitHub Agentic Workflows across 5,051 repositories to 4,112,526 run records and 562,877 nonempty execution log archives. The dataset preserves execution evidence subject to GitHub's log-retention limits and links it to repository metadata and generated workflow configurations. Illustrative cases show how the logs expose tool denials, provider failures, changes in an agent's approach, and delegation among agents. These observations enable research on execution failures, tool use, and the relationship between reported run outcomes and visible task progress. Coverage varies across workflows, and the logs provide partial observations rather than complete agent trajectories. Video: https://youtu.be/KIlfmZhHxtA

items.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
items.text: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights. The approach employs a general six-stage process with platform-specific adapters, utilizing either a PyTorch allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock to identify and read tensor allocations from video memory. items.title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
items.text: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective. We extend this paradigm to multimodal biology with Bonbon, a foundation model for molecular interactions trained on approximately 3.2 trillion tokens of paired protein-ligand sequences. From a single representation space, Bonbon exhibits three zero-shot emergent capabilities at hierarchical levels of resolution: functional (mechanism of action), residue (binding site localization, including orthosteric/allosteric discrimination), and bond (covalent versus non-covalent engagement). All three capabilities generalize to out-of-distribution complexes. Bonbon was trained on protein-ligand sequences alone, without any task-specific supervision and without structural coordinates. We conducted controlled scaling experiments across six model scales from 42M to 1.6B parameters; every capability evaluated shows a sharp jump at the largest scale on continuous metrics, even as pretraining loss decreases smoothly. items.title: DesignSpecs: A DESIGN.md Dataset of Visual Design Specifications for AI Agents
items.text: While AI agents increasingly generate and modify user interfaces, they rarely rely on a visual design specification for a certain project. The DESIGN.md format, which originated from Google's AI design tool Stitch and which was open-sourced in April 2026, addresses this gap by describing a visual identity through design tokens (such as named colors, text styles) and Markdown prose. To our knowledge, no large-scale research dataset of such design specification files exists. We present DesignSpecs, a dataset of 36,906 DESIGN.md files from 15,794 public, non-fork GitHub repositories, representing 17,240 unique file contents. We collected 613,207 files named DESIGN.md in October 2026. Because the same file name also denotes architectural plans and other design documents, we filtered those with YAML front matter, a design-system name, at least one recognized design token, and zero errors under the official linter. items.text: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. items.text: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. items.title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers
items.text: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. Here's everything going on in AI right now:

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.



5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)



6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.



7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 



8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.



9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.



10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.



11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.



Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

items.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. items.title: LLMs are Vulnerable to Malicious Requests with Indistinguishable Intent
items.text: Jailbreak attacks can circumvent the safety mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and lead to the generation of harmful or policy-violating content. We first examine eight jailbreak methods against an LLM-based filter and observe that requests resembling normal user queries tend to have higher filter pass rates than those containing obvious anomalous patterns. This observation motivates the hypothesis that resemblance to normal requests may contribute to jailbreak success. We introduce \textbf{Detail Guidance Attack (DGA)}, a framework that uses an auxiliary LLM to construct detailed requests and interacts with the victim model in a single turn. Across 11 victim models and three datasets, the complete DGA pipeline achieves high attack success rates under our automated judging criterion, including rates above 95\% in several evaluated settings. We also evaluate a DGA-aware filter and conduct a user study on everyday requests with ambiguous or dual-use intent. The survey documents differing expectations about whether models should respond; the usability costs of the filter remain to be measured.

items.text: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. items.text: Developing effective forecasting models for diverse time-series domains requires substantial expert knowledge, evidence from scientific literature on the web, and iterative experimentation. However, translating this knowledge and research experience into model designs requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions. items.text: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. items.text:
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀.



It is teaching them to stop flattening people into language names.



“Arabic.”

“English.”

“Spanish.”

...



These labels are convenient for datasets.



But humans do not speak labels.



We speak from cities, villages, families, histories, professions, memories, migrations, jokes, wounds, rituals, and relationships.



A grandmother does not speak like a government form.



A patient does not describe pain like a Wikipedia article.



A farmer, a nurse, a student, a shopkeeper, a traveler, and a child do not all speak the same “standard” version of a language.



And yet, much of modern AI still behaves as if language were  uniform, and separable from the people who use it.



This is one of the great unsolved problems in multilingual AI.



Not only translation.



𝗩𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴.

𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁.

𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿.

𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁.

𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆.



This is the global problem behind our new project:

𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮.



The name is intentional.



Alexandria was never just a city.



It was one of humanity’s boldest symbols of knowledge moving across languages, cultures, and worlds.



A place where translation was not clerical work.

It was civilization-building.



Today, we borrow that name for a new question at the heart of AI:



𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀?



For too long, Arabic has been flattened in technology.



One label: “Arabic.”

One assumed standard.

One imagined speaker.

One simplified linguistic reality.



But Arabic is not one voice.



Arabic is Cairo and Casablanca.



Amman and Muscat.

Khartoum and Tunis.

Beirut and Riyadh.

Sana’a, Tripoli, Nouakchott, Gaza, Damascus, Algiers, Doha, Manama, and beyond.



It is dialect.

It is register.

It is gendered interaction.

It is code-switching.

It is place, intimacy, politeness, humor, memory, identity, and everyday life.



So I am thrilled to share that 𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮 has been accepted to 𝗔𝗖𝗟 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗠𝗮𝗶𝗻.



𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮: 𝗔 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗜𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀



Alexandria is our largest community-built Arabic machine translation project so far: a large-scale, human-translated, multi-domain dataset designed to help AI systems translate Arabic as people actually use it.



It brings together:

📷 𝟭𝟯 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀

📷 𝟯𝟰𝗞+ 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

📷 𝟭𝟬𝟳𝗞+ 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵 📷 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝘀

📷 𝟭𝟭 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹-𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀, including healthcare, education, agriculture, legal/financial services, tourism, logistics, and workplace communication

📷 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆-𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮

📷 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿–𝗮𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

📷 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁

📷 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗼𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲-𝘀𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵, 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗦𝗔

📷 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗴𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 to support reproducibility and future community work



But Alexandria is not only a dataset.



It is a refusal.



A refusal to treat dialects as noise.



A refusal to treat “standard” language as the only legitimate language.



A refusal to build AI systems that understand the center and mishear the margins.



Dialects are not broken versions of languages.

They are knowledge systems.



They carry social meaning.

They carry identity.

They carry memory.

They carry belonging.

They carry the subtle difference between being translated and being understood.



When AI erases dialects, it does not merely make a linguistic mistake.



It erases context.

It erases communities.

It erases the conditions under which language becomes human.



Our findings show a clear gap: current LLMs can often preserve meaning reasonably well, but still struggle to generate fluent, locally authentic dialectal Arabic, especially across fine-grained sub-dialects, domains, and social contexts.



That gap matters.



It matters when a patient describes symptoms in the words that feel natural to them.



It matters when a farmer asks for advice.

It matters when a student learns.

It matters when a traveler seeks help.

It matters when public services are supposed to reach everyone, not only those who speak the “right” variety.



Alexandria is our attempt to say something plainly:



𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘀.



We need systems that can handle variation, not erase it.

Systems that can model culture, not smooth it away.

Systems that understand that linguistic diversity is not a complication to be removed.



It is the world.



This is true for Arabic.



It is also true globally, for languages with dialects, accents, registers, contact varieties, mixed codes, regional forms, Indigenous varieties, diasporic forms, youth speech, professional speech, and deeply situated cultural meanings.



In the old Alexandria, knowledge moved across languages.



With this new Alexandria, we hope to help AI move across dialects, communities, and lived realities.

This project was only possible because of a remarkable community of collaborators across the Arab world. I am deeply grateful to everyone who contributed to building, translating, validating, evaluating, and shaping this resource.

items.text: Migrating C codebases to Rust is a promising approach to securing legacy software, but existing translators do not guarantee that a translated Rust program preserves the behavior of the C program. Neither rule-based nor large language model (LLM)-based translators have been formally verified, and existing approaches to checking translation correctness are limited to testing and bounded checks, which cannot reason about all possible executions. In this work, we present R2C2, which validates C-to-Rust translation by proving in Rocq that the Rust program refines the C program, i.e., every behavior on the Rust side is also a behavior on the C side. Since no formal semantics defines the behaviors of C and Rust programs in the same terms, we prove refinement between the two programs compiled to the LLVM intermediate representation (LLVM IR). items.text: Science is producing knowledge at unprecedented scale, while artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the generation of hypotheses, analyses, and scientific outputs further. Yet increasing the volume of research does not necessarily expand the range of directions science effectively explores. We argue that science can be understood as a collective search process in which finite resources are allocated across an evolving space of possible research trajectories. Careers, funding, organization, publication, attention, and technology act as interacting selection mechanisms that shape this allocation. items.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
items.text: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. items.text: How likely is it that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) will cause human extinction or a similarly permanent disempowerment of humanity? Humans, including AI experts, frequently disagree on this question. Yet one important perspective is missing from this debate: that of AI systems themselves. We put the question to 241 large language models (LLMs) at every available reasoning setting. The models converged on a median risk of 10.0%, with the middle 90% of their estimates between 3.5% and 15.8%, far narrower than the spread among human experts. More expensive, and typically more capable, models stated higher risks; newer models showed more uniform, but not higher, risks. More reasoning barely changed the models' estimates but widened their uncertainty, mostly toward higher risk. Almost all models named loss of control over AI as the most likely cause. items.text: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. items.text: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. items.title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
items.text: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. items.title: The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agent…
items.text:
The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this.



A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit.



I'm grateful for @JensenHuang's leadership making AI agents more secure. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents.


Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang)



Today, with over 100 industry partners, we introduced the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, bringing together OpenShell and Sentry.



Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology that will advance discovery, productivity, security, health, and prosperity for generations to come.



But its full promise can only be realized when people have confidence that AI is being built to be safe and deployed with wisdom and responsibility.



This is bigger than a single product. It's the beginning of an open ecosystem to build the trust layer for safe agent systems.



Together, we are building the foundation of the AI economy.



Trust and innovation are not in conflict. Safety is how trust is earned. We must build not only the most capable AI, but the most trusted AI, so that this extraordinary technology can realize its enormous promise for the world. nvda.ws/4hcoq7m
